nameStory: This wetland wildflower gets its charming name from its distinctive drooping flower spike that curves downward like a lizard's tail. After the white flowers fade to brown in late summer, the resemblance becomes even more striking, creating a perfect scaly tail dangling from the plant.
description: Lizard's tail is a graceful wetland perennial that grows up to 3 feet tall in shallow water and soggy soils. Its heart-shaped leaves alternate up sturdy stems, topped by distinctive white flower spikes that arch and droop like curved tails. The plant forms colonies through underground stems, creating patches of these unique flowers in marshy areas throughout the growing season.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense white spikes 3-8 inches long that curve and droop dramatically downward, with tiny flowers packed tightly along the spike that later turn brown and wrinkled

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with pointed tips arranged alternately on the stem, feeling smooth and soft to the touch with prominent veining

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright stems reaching 2-4 feet tall, often growing in colonies in standing water or very wet soil, with stems feeling somewhat succulent and hollow

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Always found with its roots in water or saturated soil, never in dry locations, often alongside cattails and other marsh plants

habitat: Look for lizard's tail in wetlands, shallow ponds, stream edges, and swampy areas throughout New England's lower elevations. It thrives in standing water or permanently saturated soils, often growing alongside cattails, pickerel rush, and other marsh plants. You'll find it in both sunny and partially shaded wetlands, from roadside ditches to the edges of beaver ponds.

seasonality.spring: New heart-shaped leaves emerge from the water and wet soil, with stems growing rapidly upward as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive white flower spikes appear and curve downward in their characteristic lizard-tail shape, blooming from early to mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes turn brown and become even more tail-like, while leaves may yellow before dying back to the roots.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground stems, leaving no above-ground traces in the frozen wetland.

funFact: Beavers absolutely love munching on lizard's tail and can significantly reduce populations where they're active - it's like candy to them, making beaver ponds one of the best places to look for this plant, but also where you might find it heavily browsed down to stubs!
confusionNotes: The drooping white flower spike is so distinctive that lizard's tail is rarely confused with other plants once you see it in bloom. Before flowering, the heart-shaped leaves might remind you of some arrowhead plants, but arrowhead grows in deeper water and has distinctly arrow-shaped (not heart-shaped) leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common names like "water-dragon" and "swamp root," this plant is completely unrelated to actual lizards or dragons. Native Americans traditionally used it medicinally for reducing inflammation and fevers, though it should never be consumed without expert knowledge.
compareHints: Lizard's tail is the only member of its family (Saururaceae) that you'll encounter in New England, making it quite unique. The closest relatives are found in Asia, so there's nothing quite like it in our region. Its combination of heart-shaped leaves, wetland habitat, and distinctively curved white flower spikes makes it unmistakable once you know what to look for.
